blocks.text: One of those four birds mentioned in §. 260, which the Talmud (Joma 75b) describes as tasty, is the קיכלי, Κίχλη [kichlē], the thrush. Its flesh is extremely savory, and is especially prized on account of its bitter-pleasant taste, resulting from its eating aromatic berries.

This bird is named variously in the Talmud. It is called, first, פסיון (B. Kama 55a; Joma 75b), pl. כסיוני (Kiduschin 31a) and כסיואני (Midr. Jalkut Schimoni, Ps. fol. 98, col. 1). In the first passage it is said: The cock, the peacock and the פסיון may not be crossed with one another, even though they are raised together.
In the second passage it says: There are four kinds of tasty birds: the fieldfare, the quail, the thrush and the פסיון.

In the third passage, finally, it is said: Many a son feeds his father with כסיוני and drives him from the world through grudging, and many a one makes him do mill-work and nevertheless brings him to eternal life.

In all these passages Aruch, Buxdorf and others translate the word as pheasant, but cannot remove the difficulties that necessarily arise from this translation. First, the Talmud cannot possibly place the pheasant in one category with the thrush, fieldfare and quail, since it has not the slightest kinship with them. Second, in the first passage the pheasant cannot be meant, since it does not voluntarily mix either with the peacock or with the hen.

Rashi therefore did not let himself be misled by the similar sound of the word and translates it as: פירדיץ, Perdrix, partridge. As regards first the determination of the genus, the partridge, by its inner nature, cannot of course be counted among the quail family, for the quail is a migratory bird, whereas the partridge is a resident bird; on the other hand they are so similar externally that Theophrastus (see Bondi in Or Ester p. 296) calls the quail Perdix nana (dwarf partridge); in other respects too both birds have the same habits: they do not lay their eggs in nests but hide them on the ground in the grass (Arist. loc. cit. 6, 1, 2), both cry out during mating (l. c. 4, 9, 7), both gather their young under themselves and have no nests at all (l. c. 9, 9, 1); finally the great lustfulness of both birds is well known. To that extent it cannot seem strange that the Talmud calls the partridge a kind of quail, which, moreover, according to our explanation of סלין (§. 260), whereby those four birds are placed side by side on account of their tastiness, is not even necessary.

As for the first passage concerning the mixing of the birds, [p. 214] it is well known that partridges can be tamed and, like domestic fowl, driven about in flocks (Beumer: Popul. Naturg. p. 215); they mate voluntarily with domestic hens and, as Aristotle (De gener. 2, 4) attests, produce numerous offspring. Thus the correctness of Rashi's explanation cannot be doubted; only he explains the word in the third passage somewhat inaccurately; he says here: עוף השוב ופסיון ושמן מין שליו שירד במדבר, i.e., the פסיון is an excellent and fat bird, a kind of quail, which came (for the Israelites) in the wilderness. More precise, however, are the Tosephot, which do not mention the fatness, since the flesh of the partridge is indeed juicy, but precisely not fat (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 301).
Conclusion. The partridge is called, second, קורא.

Chulin 138b it says: If one finds a male partridge (קורא זכר, the female is called: קורא נקבה ibid. 140b) brooding the eggs, R. Elieser holds that one may not take it together with the eggs, since in this case too one must proceed according to the legal prescription (Deut. 22, 6); another, however, holds that one may take both, bird and eggs. Maimuni says: קורא is the well-known bird פרדיץ, Perdrix, in which the male broods just like the female.

This agrees completely with the statement of Aristotle; he says (loc. cit. 6, 8, 2): The partridges make two nests*); on one of them the female broods, on the other the male. Each feeds its hatched young separately. On the other hand, Rashi's explanation reads: עוף (טמא, טהור) הוא ודרכו לרבוץ על ביצי אחרים, or "It is an (unclean, or clean) bird that is wont to brood the eggs of others." Of the two readings, that of "clean" is the correct one, since the partridge is meant here; according to the other reading, "unclean," it is supposed to be the cuckoo, since Rashi elsewhere too translates קורא as cuckoo (§. 265); but this bird, although it lays its eggs in the nest of the warbler, wagtail, robin and others, never broods others' eggs, since it makes things easy for itself and does not even brood its [p. 215] own eggs.

On the other hand, the other reading correctly denotes the partridge; in the Orient the belief held concerning it that it broods others' eggs, but that the young, when they hear the voice of their real mother, leave the partridge and hasten to her (Rosenmüller: loc. cit. 4, 2, p. 394). Rashi also once (1. Sam. 26, 20) translates קירא as: פרדיץ, Perdrix, partridge.
Finally, let it be noted that Rashi (Berachoth 39a) translates פרגיות as פרדרי. Perdrix; cf., however, §. 239 on this.

The cuckoo is mentioned not in the Talmud but in the commentaries. Rashi (Chulin 62a) says: That kind of raven which is raised in houses, and which is called קוקיאה, Coucou, is wont to press food firmly to the ground with its foot and tear pieces off it with its beak.

The Tosephot (ibid. 63a. s.v. נץ) do indeed dispute that קירא means cuckoo, since the Hebrew word denotes a clean bird (ibid. 138b; see §. 264), but they leave that natural-historical statement undisputed.
